author: Joseph James
title: Patients Who Switched from Weight-Loss Shots to the Wegovy Pill Lost 4.1% of Body Weight in Three Months
text:
Patients Who Switched from Weight-Loss Shots to the Wegovy Pill Lost 4.1% of Body Weight in Three Months
People who switched from injectable weight-loss drugs to Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill lost an average of 4.1% of their body weight in the three months after switching, according to real-world data released by Novo and presented Sept. 30 at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes meeting in Milan.
The study, called OCTANE, followed 194 adults with overweight or obesity who moved from injectable semaglutide or tirzepatide to the once-daily pill. It was conducted by Novo and the telehealth company Ro. The data are early and observational, not from a randomized trial, and they did not compare switchers with people who stayed on shots.
For patients weighing whether to trade a weekly needle for a daily tablet, the findings offer a first look at what happened after the change. They do not answer whether switching works as well as staying on an injection.
Inside the OCTANE Results
The data came from de-identified records on Ro's platform as part of a research collaboration between Ro and Novo. Patients switched between Jan. 5 and Feb. 7, 2026, and started at an average weight of 221.6 pounds.
The average loss was 8.8 pounds over three months. About 41% lost at least 5% of their body weight, and the share with a body mass index of 30 or higher, the clinical cutoff for obesity, fell from 87.1% to 65.5%. Among patients with available data, 82.4% reported at least one improvement, such as better-fitting clothes or healthier eating.
The 4.1% figure measures change from the day of the switch. The study did not require patients to have lost weight on injections first, so it cannot show how much they had lost before switching.
"We innovate to meet people with obesity where they are," said Martin Holst Lange, Novo's executive vice president and chief scientific officer. He said some people choose to switch because of needle anxiety, lifestyle, or personal preference.
"What the OCTANE data showed is that a switch to oral semaglutide may be a viable path for the right patient," said Dr. Louis Aronne, director of the Comprehensive Weight Control Center at Weill Cornell Medicine and a study co-author. Aronne is a clinical adviser to Ro.
Limits Behind the Early Numbers
Novo listed several limitations. "Real-world studies evaluate associations and cannot determine causality," the company said, adding that self-reported data may be biased and results may not apply to the broader population.
One limitation stands out. Only patients who stayed on the pill for three months without a gap of more than 30 days were counted. People who stopped because of side effects, cost, or poor results were left out, which can make outcomes look better than they would for everyone who tries switching.
The analysis also did not report side effects, the doses patients took, or how many came from semaglutide versus tirzepatide. It has not been published as a full peer-reviewed paper.
The stakes for Novo are commercial as well as medical. Pills now make up about one-third of U.S. obesity prescriptions, and Novo holds more than 80% of new prescriptions for oral obesity drugs, Reuters reported. Real-world data that encourage switching could help defend that lead as Lilly's Foundayo pill competes for the same patients.
Lange went further in comments to Reuters, saying, "Clearly, a lot of patients do even better on the pill than they did on the (injectable) drugs." The study did not test that comparison. It had no injection group, so the claim reflects the company's view rather than the data.
Cost, Dosing, and the Switch Decision
The FDA approved the Wegovy pill on Dec. 22, 2025, and it reached U.S. pharmacies on Jan. 5, 2026. In the OASIS 4 trial, its 25 mg maintenance dose produced 13.6% average weight loss, compared with 2.2% for placebo, or 16.6% among people who took it as directed.
Price can shape the decision. Novo's self-pay prices for the pill are $149 a month for the 1.5 mg starting dose, $199 for 4 mg, and $299 for the 9 mg and 25 mg doses. Most doses of the injection cost $349 a month after an introductory period. Commercial insurance copays may be as low as $25.
The pill is taken daily, while the injections are weekly. Patients considering a switch should ask their prescriber which pill dose matches their current injection, how to time the change, and what side effects to expect, since nausea and vomiting are common with both forms. Severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, or signs of dehydration need prompt medical care.
Novo and Ro plan to present more data at ObesityWeek in November. Longer follow-up will be needed to know whether early weight loss after switching holds.
Key Questions Answered
What did the OCTANE study find? The 194 adults who switched from GLP-1 injections to the Wegovy pill lost an average of 4.1% of body weight, about 8.8 pounds, over three months.
Is this a clinical trial? No. It is a retrospective, real-world analysis of telehealth records conducted by Novo Nordisk and Ro, with no comparison group.
Did patients lose more on the pill than on shots? The study cannot say. It did not measure prior weight loss or compare against people who stayed on injections.
Who was included? Adults who switched from semaglutide or tirzepatide shots and stayed on the pill for three months.
How much does the Wegovy pill cost? Self-pay prices range from $149 to $299 a month, depending on dose.
Should I switch from my injection? Talk with your prescriber first. Do not change doses or stop treatment on your own.
